structure.title: Families and campaigns
structure.text: Domestic life and military action alternate across the Napoleonic years, repeatedly interrupting one another.

structure.title: Two epilogues
structure.text: The first revisits domestic life; the second develops Tolstoy's argument about historical explanation. Their reading demands differ.

people.name: Pierre Bezukhov
people.text: The awkward, illegitimate son of a rich count, educated abroad, kind and clumsy, who is looking for something worth living for.

people.name: Andrei Bolkonsky
people.text: A proud, clever prince, bored by society and by his marriage, who goes to war in 1805 hoping to find glory.

people.name: Natasha Rostova
people.text: The youngest daughter of the warm, extravagant Rostov family, full of life, who is thirteen when the novel opens.

context.title: Russian names
context.text: A person may be called by a first name, patronymic, surname, or affectionate form. The variation often signals intimacy or social distance.
context.takeaway: Different names need not mean different people.

context.title: Rank and language
context.text: French is part of aristocratic social life even as France becomes the military enemy. Speech marks belonging, education, and political loyalties.
context.takeaway: Listen for performance within polite conversation.

notice.text: Compare military plans with what participants can actually see.
notice.why: Experience on the ground tests the authority of grand explanations.

notice.text: Follow embarrassment, money, and small misunderstandings at home.
notice.why: They alter decisions that later look inevitable.

opening: Pierre inherits a fortune and discovers that everyone knows what he should do with it. Andrei goes to war hoping to escape a life that already feels wasted. Natasha is young enough to believe happiness must be just about to begin. Napoleon is approaching, but these people still have to fall in love, endure dinner parties, and decide whom to trust. Tolstoy makes their private hopes so absorbing that history arrives as it does in life, interrupting things that seemed more important.
